items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's convert the following mixed number to an improper fraction:

Content:
[MATH: {\color{red}2}\,\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{3}]

Content:
Every mixed number can be written as the sum of its whole number and fractional parts. So, our mixed number is

Content:
[MATH: {\color{red}{2}} + {\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{3}}}.]

Content:
Next, we write the whole number part [MATH: ({\color{red}{2}})] as a fraction with [MATH: 1] in the denominator:
[MATH: {\color{red}2} = {\color{red}\dfrac21}]

Content:
Then, we put this over the same denominator as the fractional part of our mixed number. So, in this case, we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 3{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {\color{red}\dfrac21} = \dfrac{{\color{red}2} \times 3}{{\color{red}{1}} \times 3} = {\color{red}{\dfrac{6}{3}}}]

Content:
Finally, we add our fractions:

Content:
[MATH: 2(1)/(3)|=; 2 + (1)/(3)|=; (6)/(3) + (1)/(3)|=; (6 + 1)/(3)|=; (7)/(3)]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 2\,\dfrac13] expressed as a mixed number is [MATH: \dfrac73.]

sections.normalized_html: Using the fact that [MATH: 5=\dfrac{30}{6},] express [MATH: 5 \,\dfrac{1}{6}] as an improper fraction.
sections.readable_text: Using the fact that [MATH: 5=\dfrac{30}{6},] express [MATH: 5 \,\dfrac{1}{6}] as an improper fraction.

sections.normalized_html:
Every mixed number can be written as the sum of its whole number and fractional parts. So, our mixed number can be written as

[MATH: 5 \, \dfrac{1}{6} = 5 + \dfrac{1}{6}.]

Now, substituting [MATH: {\color{blue}\dfrac{30}{6}}] for [MATH: {\color{blue}5}] and adding the fractions, we obtain

[MATH: 5 + (1)/(6) = (30)/(6) + (1)/(6) = (31)/(6).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Every mixed number can be written as the sum of its whole number and fractional parts. So, our mixed number can be written as

[MATH: 5 \, \dfrac{1}{6} = 5 + \dfrac{1}{6}.]

Now, substituting [MATH: {\color{blue}\dfrac{30}{6}}] for [MATH: {\color{blue}5}] and adding the fractions, we obtain

[MATH: 5 + (1)/(6) = (30)/(6) + (1)/(6) = (31)/(6).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's convert the following mixed number to an improper fraction:

Content:
[MATH: {\color{red}2}\,\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{3}]

Content:
Every mixed number can be written as the sum of its whole number and fractional parts. So, our mixed number is

Content:
[MATH: {\color{red}{2}} + {\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{3}}}.]

Content:
Next, we write the whole number part [MATH: ({\color{red}{2}})] as a fraction with [MATH: 1] in the denominator:
[MATH: {\color{red}2} = {\color{red}\dfrac21}]

Content:
Then, we put this over the same denominator as the fractional part of our mixed number. So, in this case, we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 3{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {\color{red}\dfrac21} = \dfrac{{\color{red}2} \times 3}{{\color{red}{1}} \times 3} = {\color{red}{\dfrac{6}{3}}}]

Content:
Finally, we add our fractions:

Content:
[MATH: 2(1)/(3)|=; 2 + (1)/(3)|=; (6)/(3) + (1)/(3)|=; (6 + 1)/(3)|=; (7)/(3)]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 2\,\dfrac13] expressed as a mixed number is [MATH: \dfrac73.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Converting to an Improper Fraction Given the Whole Number Representation

Example Prompt:
Using the fact that [MATH: 5=\dfrac{30}{6},] express [MATH: 5 \,\dfrac{1}{6}] as an improper fraction.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Every mixed number can be written as the sum of its whole number and fractional parts. So, our mixed number can be written as

[MATH: 5 \, \dfrac{1}{6} = 5 + \dfrac{1}{6}.]

Now, substituting [MATH: {\color{blue}\dfrac{30}{6}}] for [MATH: {\color{blue}5}] and adding the fractions, we obtain

[MATH: 5 + (1)/(6) = (30)/(6) + (1)/(6) = (31)/(6).]

Item 5 — Example: Converting a Mixed Number to an Improper Fraction

Example Prompt:
What improper fraction is equivalent to [MATH: 5 \,\dfrac{3}{4} ?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we write the whole number part [MATH: (5)] as a fraction with [MATH: 1] in the denominator.

[MATH: 5 = \dfrac{5}{1}]

We put this over a denominator of [MATH: 4] by multiplying the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 4{:}]

[MATH: \dfrac{5}{1} = \dfrac{5 \times 4}{1 \times 4} = \dfrac{20}{4}]

Now, we add the fractions:

[MATH: 5(3)/(4) = (20)/(4) + (3)/(4) = (23)/(4)]
